Good morning, this is Diane Whitfield, chief financial officer at Meridian Insurance. I am calling about the scenario note your team sent last week. The board meets on Thursday, and they will ask me one question only. What happens to our effective rate if the reform is approved this year. So here is what I need from you. Three scenarios, not eleven pages. If the rollout starts in January, tell me what our deferred tax looks like. If it slips to the following year, tell me what changes. And please flag any risk you see in the penalty clause of the service contract, because our legal team has raised it twice. If I were presenting this alone, I would probably get the numbers right and the story wrong. That is why I want you on the call. Thank you.

A word of advice before Thursday, from someone who has sat on the other side of that table. Clients do not want certainty, because they know you cannot give it. What they want is a shape. Three columns, one recommendation. If you open with the tax incidence and the legal reasoning, you will lose the room in ninety seconds. Start with the worst-case scenario instead, because that is the one keeping them awake, and then walk back to the base case. Say what you would do if it were your money. That single sentence is worth more than the whole model behind it. And never rule out a scenario just because it is uncomfortable. If you rule it out and it happens, nobody remembers your model. They remember that you did not mention it.

Let me walk you through three regulatory scenarios. In the base case, if the reform is approved this year, your effective rate will fall by two points. In the worst-case scenario, if the rollout is delayed, the deferred tax stays on your balance sheet for another year. If I were in your position, I would prepare the tax credit offset now. So my recommendation is simple. We run the numbers again in September, and we decide then.
